tagline: Through company coal towns to the gap below Kentucky’s highest summit
intro: KY 160 follows Looney Creek through Benham and Lynch before climbing Black Mountain in tight bends. The scenic highway covers 10.341 miles from the Looney Creek Bridge at Benham’s western limits to the Virginia line. Kentucky’s Transportation Cabinet records its designation on June 13, 2000, with a route description linking the two towns and the mountain crossing. Black Mountain supports Northern Hardwood Forest at its higher elevations, with rare plants including Red Elderberry and Hobblebush.

Coal companies shaped the towns along this climb. Wisconsin Steel, an International Harvester subsidiary, founded Benham in 1912; U.S. Coal and Coke, a U.S. Steel subsidiary, laid out Lynch in 1917 to house miners. Benham’s major buildings date from 1919 to 1928, when the growing town replaced its original structures. As mining became less labor-intensive, Lynch’s population fell sharply during the 1960s and 1970s. The rail lines to both towns were officially abandoned in 1996.

Begin at the Looney Creek Bridge and take Benham’s Main Street east into Lynch. The valley lies between Looney Ridge to the north and Benham Spur to the south. Beyond Lynch, KY 160 climbs southeast to the state line at 3,700 feet. Black Mountain’s 4,145-foot summit is a separate excursion from that gap.

moments.title: Benham
moments.text: Benham’s historic center contains a generation of replacement buildings. Wisconsin Steel, a subsidiary of International Harvester, founded the town in 1912; its major buildings followed between 1919 and 1928 as Benham grew. Mining declined during the Great Depression, leaving the district representative of that main period of development. Ten buildings and a public park make up the historic district, including the company store, hospital, theatre and firehouse. The former company store now houses the Kentucky Coal Museum. KY 160 runs through this company-town setting as Main Street, continuing east toward Lynch.

moments.title: Lynch
moments.text: Lynch was planned as a home for coal workers in 1917 by U.S. Coal and Coke, a subsidiary of U.S. Steel. It took its name from company head Thomas Lynch. By the 1940s, 10,000 people lived here, with a hospital and movie theater among the town’s amenities. The shift to mining methods requiring fewer workers brought steep population losses in the 1960s and 1970s. The historic district listed in 2003 included 298 contributing buildings, four structures and a site. The city occupies Looney Creek’s valley between Looney Ridge and Benham Spur, at an elevation of 1,716 feet.

moments.title: Black Mountain
moments.text: The highway crosses Black Mountain below Kentucky’s highest summit, which reaches 4,145 feet. An abandoned metal fire lookout tower marks the summit; its cab and wooden steps are missing. In 1998, Jericol Mining petitioned to use mountaintop removal in the Black Mountain area. The summit itself was not directly threatened, but protesters objected because of the mountain’s status as the state’s highest point. Kentucky purchased the summit’s mineral and timber rights in 1999, preventing future large-scale mining. At higher elevations, the mountain supports Northern Hardwood Forest, including rare plants such as Red Elderberry and Hobblebush.

practical: Lynch: KY 160 is signposted closed to tractor-trailers between Lynch and the Virginia state line. (checked 2026-10-11)
